A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DrVoice. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

before.justification: v2 reports original DrVoice benchmark results, component ablations, grouping experiments, and data-scaling results in Tables 2–5 and Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark and ablation results, including additional training-strategy, data-quality, and forgetting experiments in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.3 replace HuBERT tokenization and direct token-to-HiFi-GAN synthesis with S3Tokenizer and speaker-conditioned flow matching followed by HiFi-GAN. Figure 1 also removes the discrete-token branch from user speech inputs. v3 introduces Core-Cocktail training: high-learning-rate fine-tuning, parameter merging with the base LLM, and low-learning-rate fine-tuning. The grouping/SRH architecture and CoM-Mixing remain.

E1.justification: Evaluation expands beyond Llama Questions and Web Questions to instruction following, refusal behavior, real-speech interaction, and reasoning through OpenAudioBench, VoiceBench, UltraEval-Audio, and Big Bench Audio. The original QA tasks remain within the expanded suites. Training adds real-speech ASR corpora, while Appendix C evaluates additional instruction datasets, including coding and mathematics data.

E2.justification: The overlapping Llama/Web comparisons add Step-Audio2-Mini and remove comparators including Moshi, MinMo, VITA-Audio, and Stream-Omni. Table 3 replaces the previous speech-quality comparator roster with MiniCPM-o 2.6, Baichuan-Omni-1.5, Qwen2.5-Omni, Kimi-Audio, and Step-Audio2-Mini. Appendix C additionally uses the original Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct text model as a reference.

E3.justification: Reported pretraining decreases from 210K to 100K hours; 17.8K conversation hours are replaced by mixtures including 26K S2S and 20K S2T hours. Learning-rate schedules become two-stage, and warmup changes from 1% to 2%. New evaluations introduce G-Eval and refusal rate. Table 2 mostly uses checkpoint inference instead of literature-sourced baseline scores. The stated Qwen backbones remain unchanged despite revised size labels.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds comparisons of training stages, instructional-data mixtures, ASR augmentation, and retention versus forgetting after text fine-tuning across multiple corpora (Tables 6, 8–9). Existing component ablations, grouping-factor experiments, and data-scaling analyses are retained: v2 Tables 5 and 4 become v3 Tables 4 and 7, and Figures 2–3 move to the appendix.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: v3 replaces the two-QA headline results with expanded results, including overall scores of 69.24 on OpenAudioBench and 66.3 on Big Bench Audio. Table 3 changes DrVoice's UTMOS/ASR-WER entries from 3.86/6.75 to 4.29/11.2 under a revised pipeline and benchmark collection, preventing a controlled performance comparison. Appendix C adds numerous training and forgetting results; the original component and grouping ablation values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds the mathematical definition of the merged model, Mr = alpha M1 + (1 - alpha) M0. The existing joint-generation, grouping, ungrouping, and loss equations (1–8) remain unchanged. Neither version contains theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: v3 adds Core-Cocktail training for LLM knowledge retention as a principal contribution. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from SOTA spoken-QA performance with relatively little data to SOTA on OpenAudioBench and Big Bench Audio, with comparable performance on VoiceBench and UltraEval-Audio among approximately 7B models.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations connecting training-stage recovery, instructional-data quality, ASR augmentation, and selective forgetting to model performance. The speech-quality limitation changes from inadequate tokenization and naturalness to weaker speech-text alignment than Qwen2.5-Omni, hypothesized to arise from SRH lacking explicit text input. Full-duplex interaction and broader multimodality remain future directions.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 and Appendix A newly specify frozen tokenizer/detokenizer components, a 2K sequence limit, interpolation weight alpha = 0, unit loss weights, and stage-specific learning rates. Reported hardware changes from 32 to 64 A800 GPUs, and v3 documents WER-based synthetic-data selection. The explicit v2 promise to release all code and checkpoints disappears; neither PDF establishes actual release availability.

R1.justification: The tokenization discussion shifts from HuBERT's lightweight, diffusion-free synthesis to S3Tokenizer/CosyVoice and SenseVoice. v3 credits LM-Cocktail for parameter merging and adds references for Step-Audio2, VoiceBench, G-Eval, and ASR corpora. The main text-driven versus joint-model taxonomy and positioning of dual-resolution modeling remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, results discussion, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. Section 3.3 broadens into Training Strategy, main results and ablations become separate subsections, and existing implementation details, prompts, analyses, and future-work material are reorganized into Appendices A–D.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn with revised input pathways and a more compact arrangement. Table 2 changes from model rows with two QA datasets to model columns with four benchmark blocks. New Tables 6, 8, and 9 display training/data analyses; existing grouping and prompt tables are relocated or reformatted, and Figures 2–3 are resized and moved to Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 supports a broad voice-conversation claim mainly through two QA benchmarks and literature-sourced comparator scores. v3 substantially strengthens the evidence through instruction-following, refusal, real-speech, and reasoning evaluations, mostly direct checkpoint comparisons, and explicit data-quality/forgetting analyses against the text backbone (Tables 6, 8–9). Some earlier comparators are dropped, uncertainty reporting remains absent, and the merging effect is insufficiently isolated. Nevertheless, the broader evaluation and diagnostic analyses substantially improve the paper's empirical foundation.
